articles.title_zh: At least 68 people dead in Spain's second major train crash this year
articles.content_orig:
BARCELONA, Spain — At least 68 people were killed and 68 injured when two high-speed trains collided in central Spain on Wednesday, sending carriages careering off the tracks, in the second major accident on the same line in less than a year.
“We heard a massive roar, a truly enormous thud that went on for 10 seconds, as if the train were about to derail,” one passenger, Miguel, told Spain’s COPE radio, adding that he was traveling with several colleagues in the rear car of one of the trains.
“Through the right-hand window, we could see a wrecked train — I imagine it must have been the other one,” he added.
Pictures showed several carriages lying on their sides next to the tracks and others twisted at angles, their wheels sheared off.  Debris was strewn around the scene of the accident in the countryside in the province of Toledo.
As rescue teams continued to search through the wreckage ‌of ​the ‌derailed ⁠carriages, the Castilla-La Mancha ‌regional government said ‌68 people had been killed and 68 injured. Together the two trains were carrying more than 500 passengers.
Several U.S. citizens were among the injured, according to a State Department spokesperson, who said the U.S. is continuing to work with local authorities to identify all Americans involved and provide them consular assistance.
“We extend our deepest condolences to the families and loved ones of all those affected,” the spokesperson said. “We encourage U.S. citizens in the area to notify loved ones of their safety and monitor local media for updates.”
At the site of the crash on Wednesday, Prime Minister of Spain Pedro Sánchez said: “The government of Spain and the whole state are with the victims and also with the families of the victims.”
Sánchez, who is facing a snap election next month, said the government was investigating the cause of the crash and any failures, vowing action “if there has been negligence.”
He said that the country must restore confidence in its high-speed rail network, with the crash coming after a separate disaster on the same rail line killed 46 people in January. “It is unacceptable for a country like Spain to have two high-speed accidents in less than a year,” he said.
Spain’s transport minister Oscar Puente said Wednesday’s crash ⁠occurred after a state-owned Renfe high-speed train was authorized ⁠to ​continue its ⁠journey despite an active red ⁠signal and ⁠a stationary ‌train from private rail company Iryo on the tracks ahead.
Addressing ‌reporters in ‌Madrid, Puente said ⁠the red signal was issued due to a computer communications failure which automatically stopped ‌traffic. An erroneous ​decision was ‌made ⁠to restart the ⁠Renfe train, breaking protocol, he said.
Locals rushed to the scene of the accident, which has prompted a major national emergency response and raised questions about the safety and security of Spain’s high-speed rail infrastructure, which had previously been hailed as among the most sophisticated in Europe.
Esther Padilla, spokeswoman for the Castilla La Mancha region, told state broadcaster TVE that the trains were heading in the same direction from Madrid to Seville when one ran into the tail of the other, which had stopped on the line.
She added that some 397 people had been traveling on the Renfe train and 147 people on the Iryo train.
Spain’s royal family who said they shared “in the grief of the families and loved ones of those who lost their lives.”
Spanish political parties said Wednesday they would briefly pause campaigning ahead of next month’s general election. Spain’s football federation also said it would postpone some of its Copa del Rey soccer fixtures, following the collision.
Aerial footage shows aftermath of deadly crash
Juan Manuel Moreno, the president of the Andalusian regional government, said on X that there would be three days of mourning in the region.
The full scale of the disaster remains unclear but officials said an emergency phone line had been set up for families of the victims; local blood banks had also made appeals for donations.
Manuel Galan, the mayor of the nearby municipality of Urda, said he had been asked by emergency services to prepare a sports hall to accommodate the injured.
Eduarda, a passenger on the Iryo train, told Spain’s Cadena SER radio that she felt a strong impact that threw her forward and she initially thought the train had made an emergency stop.
After climbing down an embankment to safety, she said she saw part of the train hanging down the slope and a fire in one carriage. “I saw dead people,” she added.
Salvador Arriza, a 62-year-old employee of Airbus, was travelling to the rear of the Renfe train.
He told the Reuters news agency the carriage ended up “completely wrecked, with seats being ripped out.”
“I was lucky because I was in a backward-facing seat, and the impact pushed me into it,” he added. “After the first hit I was disoriented, but the worst thing was that the train then kept moving for quite some time from the inertia and that’s when I thought something would happen to me.”
Emergency responders, including a helicopter, police and ambulances, arrived within about 20 minutes, she said.
Spain has the largest high-speed rail network in Europe for trains moving more than 155 mph, with more than 1,900 miles of track, according to the European Union.
Adela Suliman is a breaking-news editor and reporter for NBC News in London.
Daniella Silva is a national reporter for NBC News, focusing on immigration.
Abigail Williams is a producer and reporter for NBC News covering the State Department.

articles.title_orig: A U.K. Budget With ‘Breathing Space’ in a Time of Rising Energy Costs
articles.title_zh: A U.K. Budget With ‘Breathing Space’ in a Time of Rising Energy Costs
articles.content_orig:
The U.K.'s finance minister John Healey delivered his first fiscal budget on Wednesday, announcing funding for defense, AI initiatives and measures designed to ease cost-of-living pressures.
The Autumn Budget included dozens of measures aimed largely at easing rising costs for Britain's population, but Healey was careful not to risk the ire of markets, which responded broadly positively to his plans.
As a net energy importer, the U.K. is vulnerable to external energy shocks.
Inflation has risen sharply this year, with surging fuel costs driving the annual inflation rate to 3.5% in September. Markets expect the Bank of England to hike interest rates next month, while government borrowing costs have risen sharply this year.
The U.K. government, led by Prime Minister Andy Burnham, had promised to alleviate economic pressures ahead of the budget.
On Wednesday, Healey said he would deliver "breathing space" for families, saying the country needs "radical change on energy," and citing the inflationary impact of the U.S.-Iran war — a conflict he said "we did not want."
His measures included the removal of standing charges on household gas heating bills, the extension of a tax break on electricity for millions of households through July 2027, and £100 ($133) checks for those living in the four lowest local housing tax bands. This will cost £2.6 billion.
Healey said tariffs would be removed on over 100 grocery products, a policy announced before the budget was officially unveiled. Small business relief from business rates — a tax on commercial premises — would be extended to include more companies in the hospitality, retail and leisure sectors. Other measures included £15 million to provide books for children, funding aimed at reducing homelessness and support for people to purchase their first home.
The U.K.'s minimum wage will rise by 3.9%, while a planned cut to tax-free savings thresholds was canceled.
But Healey also pledged to bring down the welfare bill, pointing to reforms to pensions and sickness benefits.
But he said he would not "write off a million young people [or] see disabled people suffer the indignities of a system that has been found 'not fit for purpose.'"
The U.K.'s welfare bill, which reached 10.7% of UK GDP in 2024/25, has been a contentious issue in recent years. Previous finance minister Rachel Reeves watered down her own plans to cut welfare spending after a rebellion from lawmakers within her party.
Healey also announced investments in developing — and regulating — the U.K.'s artificial intelligence industry.
"Nowhere is the necessary role for the state clearer than in artificial intelligence," he said, as he announced hundreds of millions of pounds in funding for AI security and sovereignty.
He announced a "covenant" for data centers in the country, with "strict tests" they must meet: "To invest in local communities, create local jobs and protect local water supplies. In return, critical data centers will get the grid connections they need, and, where necessary, be allowed to build onsite generation while they wait," Healey said.
Healey also announced tax breaks for founders, including a reduced capital gains tax rate on gains of up to £10 million.
Cash would also be injected into various regional hubs, Healey said, to "unleash Britain's innovation power."
The budget also included £10 billion of additional economic and military support for Ukraine .
"Today we send a clear message to Moscow: Britain will stand with Ukraine for as long as it takes," he said. More funding would go to defense, he added, to ensure the country can meet its NATO spending commitments.
"At the Spending Review next year, I confirm that I will set out the details of how we will meet our NATO commitment to spend 3.5% of GDP on defense by 2035, with a target date for 3% in 2030," he said. "In this new era of threat, the demands on U.K. defense are rising."
Healey said his spending plans complied with the so-called fiscal rules set by his predecessor. Under those rules, the government's day-to-day spending must be funded by tax revenues rather than borrowing, and debt must be declining as a share of GDP.
Alongside the budget announcements on Wednesday, the U.K.'s Office for Budget Responsibility forecast that the government would have £15 billion of fiscal headroom by the 2029/30 financial year.
"Despite global challenges, this Budget puts us on track to eliminate the current budget deficit and get Britain's finances into the black within three years," Healey told lawmakers in parliament before unveiling the full details of his fiscal shake-up.
The OBR forecast on Wednesday that national debt as a share of GDP would rise slightly to 83.8% next year, before steadily declining until it reaches 81.7% of GDP by the 2032 financial year. It also raised its growth forecast for the U.K., saying it now expects the economy to expand by 1.2% this year, 1% in 2027 and 1.6% in 2028.
Yields on U.K. government bonds, known as gilts, fell as Healey spoke. By 1:50 p.m. in London (9.50 a.m. ET), the yield on the benchmark 10-year gilt was 2 basis points lower at 5.323%.
Sterling was marginally lower against the U.S. dollar, and 0.2% lower versus the euro .
Healey said Wednesday that he would raise revenue "from those who can afford to pay."
"No tax rises on wages or dividends," he said. "Cutting taxes for millions of families and businesses."
Banks, gambling businesses and vape shops would be taxed to help pay for the new measures, he announced.
Healey — who earlier this month called Britain's banks the "jewel" in the country's economic crown — said the bank surcharge would now be raised by 3%, bringing it to 6%.
Healey said the U.K.'s "world-leading banks" make a "huge contribution" to the country — and he was now asking them to fund the "breathing space" for Britain's households.
The temporary measure will be implemented in January and end 15 months later.
The scale of tax hikes was not as severe as some in the sector had feared, and shares in London-listed lenders moved higher on the announcement.
Shares in U.K. banks rose. Barclays were last seen 3.3% higher, while Lloyds Banking Group rose more than 2.6%. NatWest Group was up 2.5%.
JPMorgan Chase , whose CEO Jamie Dimon joined bankers lobbying against additional U.K. taxes last month, said in a statement that "to single out this industry for additional taxes again, one of the UK's biggest generators of growth and jobs, lacks principle."
"It also overlooks that the banking industry operates in a highly competitive global marketplace," a company spokesperson said.
Dimon has previously suggested it may rethink the multibillion-dollar buildout of its new headquarters in London's Canary Wharf financial district if the government is "hostile" to banks.
The company said on Wednesday that it is "committed" to the U.K.
— CNBC's Hugh Leask contributed to this report.

articles.title_zh: Israel Election Results Live Updates: Exit Polls Show No Clear Winner
articles.content_orig:
Jerusalem 6:42 p.m. Oct. 28
Isabel Kershner Johnatan Reiss Aaron Boxerman Qasim Nauman and Leo Sands
Israel’s political leaders were poised for weeks of negotiations over the shape of the next government, as initial results on Wednesday showed no clear winner in a tightly fought election that many have described as a make-or-break moment for the country.
If neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s hard-line alliance nor an opposition bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot win enough seats to form a government, both would need to find support from outside their blocs for backing as prime minister.
By Wednesday afternoon, election officials had counted more than 70 percent of ballots. Those votes, alongside exit polls, indicate that neither bloc would reach the 61 seats needed to secure a straightforward majority in the Knesset, Israel’s Parliament.
Some of Mr. Netanyahu’s allies are floating the idea that he could join Mr. Eisenkot and other centrists to form a broad unity government to stay in power. For Mr. Netanyahu, the long-serving prime minister who remains as a caretaker until a government is formed, that would be a comfortable scenario, as long as he remained on top.
His primary rival, Mr. Eisenkot, faces a dilemma of his own: He has denounced Mr. Netanyahu as unfit to lead Israel, but he has also objected to partnering with Arab parties in a potential coalition. The two Arab parties are projected to win as many as 17 seats — a remarkable show of strength that could make them Mr. Eisenkot’s only path to toppling Mr. Netanyahu.
On Wednesday, Mr. Eisenkot did not explicitly mention the Arab parties and instead pledged to build “a stable Zionist government.”
Most of the votes were expected to be counted by Wednesday, though the final tally could take days. Lengthy negotiations could follow as political parties try to assemble a governing majority. If those talks fail, the country could head to a second round of elections — a scenario that has played out before. For Mr. Netanyahu, running down the clock in the hope of securing a stronger showing in a fresh election could be his strongest shot at retaining his role as prime minister.
The uncertainty did not stop the leading candidates from making triumphant late-night speeches to their supporters.
Mr. Eisenkot, a former Israeli military chief of staff, struck a defiant tone toward Mr. Netanyahu, saying: “Tonight we got the answer: The public opted for change.”
A few hours later, Mr. Netanyahu told supporters that his party, Likud, had emerged as the largest in Israel. “We must form a strong right-wing government,” he said.
Here’s what else we are covering:
Herzog’s role: President Isaac Herzog of Israel holds a largely ceremonial position, except after national elections, when it falls to him to select a potential prime minister. Read more ›
More votes: The exit polls do not reflect the hundreds of thousands of votes cast at special polling stations, including at military bases, hospitals, prisons and embassies. In Israel’s 2022 election, those votes tended to favor Mr. Netanyahu and his allies.
Regional implications: Israel’s neighbors in the Middle East had little hope that the election would fundamentally change Israel’s security doctrine, which has hardened since the Hamas-led attacks of Oct. 7, 2023. Read more ›
Initial results: The 70 percent of the votes counted indicate that Mr. Netanyahu’s coalition will receive about 54 seats, Mr. Eisenkot’s bloc will get roughly 49, and the Arab parties will reach 17. But the numbers could still easily shift.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party is persisting with unproven allegations that Israel’s Arab voters have “stolen the elections.” Israel’s official elections committee has said there was no indication of widespread irregularities in the election on Tuesday. On Wednesday, the Likud again said that Arab parties — which are expected to receive a historically high number of parliamentary seats — had stolen the vote and called for the police and intelligence services to investigate.
Analysts say that Netanyahu is trying to de-legitimize votes by Arab citizens of Israel, fearing that his leading Jewish Israeli opponents might try to link up with the newly empowered Arab political bloc in an effort to unseat him.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel fell short of outright victory on Tuesday night. But he has still emerged with a good chance of clinging to power.
Mr. Netanyahu, 77, has plenty of political blessings to count after the vote. His Likud party is set to remain the largest in the Israeli Parliament, defying the pre-election polls. His rivals, led by the former general Gadi Eisenkot, secured far less support and have been left more divided than expected.
Analysts say the result, with neither bloc securing enough votes to form a clear majority, could easily lead to weeks or months of political gridlock — a scenario that suits Mr. Netanyahu just fine. He will remain in charge as caretaker prime minister until a new government is formed or new elections have to be held.
It is a remarkable turnaround for Mr. Netanyahu, whose critics blamed him for failing to prevent the Hamas-led attack on Oct. 7, 2023, the deadliest day in Israeli history. A consummate political survivor of more than three decades in Israeli politics, Mr. Netanyahu is famous for out-negotiating and manipulating almost every opponent who has tried to end his rule.
“Netanyahu is still in the driver’s seat,” said Natan Sachs, an expert on Israeli politics at the Middle East Institute, a Washington-based research group. “He’s still in control of most events, and that’s where he likes to be.”
Mr. Netanyahu, the longest serving prime minister in Israeli history, still has some headaches. The hard-line coalition he formed in 2022 — the most far-right in Israeli history — is set to lose its majority in Israel’s 120-member Parliament.
Mr. Netanyahu could also end up losing if Mr. Eisenkot, whose bloc trails the prime minister’s coalition by several seats, chooses to work with the Arab parties that performed better than ever to oust him.
But Mr. Eisenkot is likely to struggle to form such an alliance, given how Israeli public opinion has shifted since the Oct. 7 attacks. Even though Arab leaders in Israel generally condemned the attacks, many Jewish Israelis still regard partnering with them as unacceptable.
“Netanyahu knew he was going to have a weaker bloc. But he knew that his goal, even if he couldn’t get a 61-seat majority, would be to prevent his rivals from forming a government,” said Mazal Mualem, who has written a biography of Mr. Netanyahu. “And it seems he’s succeeded.”
All this was hard to imagine just three years ago. Mr. Netanyahu’s public standing plunged after the Oct. 7 attacks, when 1,200 in Israel were killed and 250 were taken hostage, igniting the war in Gaza. Even fervent supporters of the prime minister feared his time in office would end because of his failure to prevent the catastrophe.
Mr. Netanyahu, however, has tenaciously clambered his way back without accepting any responsibility for the devastating security lapse. Instead, he blamed the assault on Israeli security chiefs, launched a series of military campaigns in Lebanon and Iran that killed some of Israel’s most significant foes, and ran his electoral campaign focused on amplifying fears of Israel’s Arab parties.
On Tuesday, a swath of Jewish Israelis threw their support behind him, defying Mr. Netanyahu’s critics at home and abroad. Qatari mediators on Sunday handed Iran a new draft deal to end the war, the Reuters news agency reported, citing an official briefed on the negotiations.
Tehran is considering the proposal and set to respond by the end of the week, the agency reported Wednesday.
The source added that there were concerns in Tehran before the meeting on Sunday that Israel could resume its bombardment of Iran this week.
The cost of the Iran war has risen to an estimated $47 billion, according to an estimate from the U.S. military's Central Command obtained by CBS News Tuesday.
Like previous estimates, it does not include damage to U.S. military bases in the Middle East. The bulk of the cost, $29 billion, is for replacing expended munitions.
According to a report released by the nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office in September, the Iran war could cost approximately $2 billion to $3 billion per month for as long as it continues.
Exit polls from Israel's major television networks project that a majority of Israelis voted against Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's coalition in Tuesday's election, but his Likud party still emerged as the largest party among all the contenders. Neither bloc, Netanyahu or the opposition, has a clear majority.
While Netanyahu appears to have won fewer votes than his main challenger, according to the early exit polls, both candidates will likely struggle to cobble together a coalition.
One or the other would need to obtain majority support in Israel's 120-seat parliament, known as the Knesset, in order to form a government.
Israel's two Arab parties won more seats in parliament than in any previous election. That electoral success comes after what some Arab voters told CBS News was a difficult time for them in the country under the hard-right government of Netanyahu, prompting a historic turnout for the minority community.
Both Netanyahu and those opposing him have vowed not to form a government reliant on Arab parties, arguing it would endanger the country if they gain enough seats to influence Israel's engagement in its myriad conflicts. Arab citizens of Israel are around 20% of the population.

articles.title_orig: FDA scientists opposed the Trump administration’s effort to ease peptides access
articles.title_zh: FDA scientists opposed the Trump administration’s effort to ease peptides access
articles.content_orig:
The Department of Health and Human Services is giving compounding pharmacies a temporary green light to make six peptides while the agency continues to work on a formal rule change.
In a notice filed Wednesday, the agency said it would exercise “enforcement discretion,” meaning it will not take legal action against compounding pharmacies that make the six unapproved peptides. In practice, that means these pharmacies can start offering them now, even though the peptides aren’t yet on the Food and Drug Administration’s list of ingredients compounding pharmacies are allowed to make.
The six peptides are BPC-157, epitalon, KPV, MOTS-c, semax and TB-500.
They’ve been promoted online as treatments for everything from faster healing to younger-looking skin and a longer lifespan. None are approved by the FDA, and the agency’s own scientists concluded there is insufficient data to prove they are safe and effective.
The FDA said compounding pharmacies must certify the identity and purity of the compounds. They must also now report side effects, which was not previously mandated.
The move comes as a growing “gray market” has sprung up around peptides, where retailers sell them labeled “for research use only,” a legal workaround that lets them claim they aren’t meant for humans. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and others have argued that allowing peptides to be compounded would move people away from this gray market and toward safer products.
“Under President Trump’s leadership, HHS is working to put prevention and patient safety at the center of health care—and that includes confronting the risks of black-market peptides,” Emily Hilliard, an HHS spokesperson, said in a statement.
Dr. Peter Lurie, a former FDA official who now leads the Center for Science in the Public Interest watchdog group, said the FDA was essentially “turning a blind eye” to widen access to drugs that have not been proven to work.
Compounding pharmacies generally may use only ingredients the FDA has added to an official list known as the bulk drugs substances list. Adding an ingredient requires the FDA to propose a rule, take public comment and issue a final rule, a process that can take several months.
The agency took a step toward that process in July, when an FDA advisory panel narrowly voted in favor of adding six peptides to the bulk list. The panel included six new appointees with ties to the peptide industry and another who is the son of a U.S. representative who has pushed Kennedy to make peptides more available. (During that meeting, some committee members expressed concerns that the recommendation could make it harder for the FDA to say no to other unapproved drugs in the future.)
On Tuesday and Wednesday, the FDA was scheduled to meet outside groups, including Medivant Healthcare, a compounding pharmacy that offers peptides, according to Reginfo.gov , a federal website that tracks government regulations.
Shabbir Safdar, executive director of the Partnership for Safe Medicines, which researches the dangers of counterfeit medicines, said both the enforcement discretion and upcoming rule change would expose Americans to “untested dangerous substances.”
“Imagine what it means for the nation’s top drug regulator to announce they won’t enforce the laws on people making completely untested compounds and distributing them to the public,” Safdar said.
Berkeley Lovelace Jr. is a health and medical reporter for NBC News. He covers the Food and Drug Administration, with a special focus on Covid vaccines, prescription drug pricing and health care. He previously covered the biotech and pharmaceutical industry with CNBC.

US military says the restrictions on the electric vehicles at Kadena airbase also apply to delivery drivers and taxis
One of America’s biggest overseas military bases has banned vehicles made by the Chinese electric vehicle maker BYD over security concerns, the US military in Japan said on Tuesday.
The ban, which went into effect this week at Kadena airbase on the southern Japanese island of Okinawa , has fueled speculation that similar measures could be taken at other US military facilities as part of Washington’s crackdown on Chinese technology it suspects of being used to collect sensitive information.
“These vehicles present an unacceptable and unmitigable risk to our personnel and our mission,” Lieut Col Alli Stormer, a spokesperson for the US air force 18th Wing at Kadena, said in a statement.
The restrictions apply to all BYD vehicles, including privately owned cars, taxis and delivery vehicles, reports said, adding that security personnel stationed at the base’s gates had been instructed to block BYD vehicles and instruct drivers to turn around.
Kadena, the biggest US air force base east Asia, would be directly involved in responding to a crisis involving China , Russia or North Korea .
Its inventory includes the powerful Typhon missile system, which is said to be capable of firing Tomahawk missiles as far as 1,600km, putting parts of China and Russia within striking distance. Kadena also hosts fighter planes and aircraft used for mid-air refuelling, surveillance and reconnaissance, according to its website.
The move comes amid concerns of potential information leaks via vehicle-mounted technologies such as cameras, sensors and GPS devices, South Korea’s Yonhap news agency said.
American military officials have not identified a specific threat, but the ban is part of wider measures taken by the US and other western countries to restrict Chinese smart technology in vehicles, mobile phones and other devices they fear could be used to “spy” on their owners.
In June the Pentagon added BYD to a list of 188 Chinese firms it believes have ties to the country’s military, drawing a protest from Beijing. The blacklist also includes the automaker Nio, e-commerce firm Alibaba and internet company Baidu.
The US defence department banned the sale and use of smartphones from Chinese companies Huawei and ZTE at military bases worldwide in 2018, again citing security concerns.
China has imposed similar restrictions on US-made Tesla vehicles. In 2021, it barred them from some government compounds due to security concerns over ⁠cameras installed on the vehicles. Beijing removed that restriction in 2024 after Tesla won an endorsement from the country’s top auto industry association.
BYD, which has not immediately responded publicly to the Kadena ban, overtook Tesla as the world’s biggest seller of battery-electric vehicles in 2025.
It is now expanding overseas, including in the world’s fourth-biggest auto market, Japan , where in July it launched its Racco electric minicar in the hope that the small, cost-efficient vehicle would carve out a place in a market dominated by domestic brands.

articles.title_zh: Ethiopia says it received Russian Su-35 jets, S-400 air defence systems to follow
articles.content_orig:
Ethiopia has received 12 Russian Su-35 fighter jets and will also acquire four S-400 air defence batteries, Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has announced.
Abiy made the announcement on X on Wednesday during a visit to Moscow for the two-day Russia-Africa Summit, where Russia is seeking closer security and economic ties with African countries.
The acquisition comes as Ethiopian forces fight renewed battles with rebels in northern Tigray and a separate rebellion in the neighbouring Amhara region.
The prime minister said the warplanes had arrived a year earlier than expected under an existing agreement with Moscow, thanking Russian President Vladimir Putin for helping speed up the delivery.
He gave no date for the arrival of the S-400 batteries, designed to shoot down aircraft and missiles.
Abiy said on Wednesday that the new equipment would strengthen Ethiopia’s ability to “preemptively deter aggression”.
In a second X post later that day, he described the jets as newly deployed and said they would defend Ethiopian airspace.
The announcement is the latest sign of Russia ‘s growing military partnership with Ethiopia, following a series of agreements in recent years.
The two governments signed a military cooperation agreement in Addis Ababa in July 2021 aimed at improving the Ethiopian armed forces’ training and technology.
In January, defence publication Janes reported that Ethiopia had displayed newly acquired Russian Yak-130 advanced jet trainers during celebrations marking its air force’s 90th anniversary.
Russia supplied 15 percent of Africa’s imports of major weapons between 2021 and 2025, making it the continent’s third-largest supplier, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute.
Moscow has sought closer military and economic ties with African countries while facing Western sanctions over its war in Ukraine.
The Russia-Africa Summit, which began on Wednesday, brings African leaders together for talks on trade, investment and security.
The announcement follows a major shift in the fighting in Tigray, where government troops and allied forces entered the regional capital Mekelle on October 4 after fighters from the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) withdrew.
The TPLF, an armed group that previously governed the region, has suffered further territorial losses as government forces advanced into other towns.
Addis Ababa has since appointed a six-month caretaker administration for Tigray, but the fighting has not stopped.
A TPLF commander called for continued resistance in a television broadcast last week, while the group has also claimed attacks against government-aligned troops in northwestern Tigray on Wednesday.
The renewed war has effectively undone a peace agreement signed in Pretoria, South Africa, in November 2022 that ended two years of fighting, which researchers at Belgium’s Ghent University estimate killed about 500,000 civilians.
Government forces are also battling Fano, an Amhara armed group that has been fighting federal troops since 2023.

articles.title_orig: Meloni furious as Italian judge frees man accused of inciting violent protests
articles.title_zh: Meloni furious as Italian judge frees man accused of inciting violent protests
articles.content_orig:
Yousef Sihar, an Italian citizen of Moroccan descent  | Photo: Social media
Italian police arrested a 30-year-old pro-Palestinian activist on Saturday. The suspect allegedly organized the stormy protests across the country and incited violence and terrorism during the demonstrations. According to Italian media, the suspect was known to the country's domestic intelligence service after founding an organization that spread propaganda identified with Hamas . The arrest came as thousands of young people took to the streets in many Italian cities and clashed with police. Protests have also continued in France, where clashes were recorded in several cities, and in Barcelona, where hundreds of young people rioted and looted stores.
The suspect, Yousef Sihar, is an Italian citizen of Moroccan descent. According to Italy's Interior Ministry, Sihar created the chat group that gave rise to the October 17 Movement and also wrote its manifesto. The movement takes its name from the date of the previous Saturday, when the protest in France spiraled out of control.
According to La Repubblica , Sihar was located at a friend's apartment in Milan and taken in for questioning shortly before the time the movement was supposed to announce the protest locations. Cyber police had tracked him for several days together with the counterterrorism unit, and Meta gave investigators the IP address of the movement's Instagram page. That evening, the Milan prosecutor's office ordered his arrest. ANSA reported that he is suspected of incitement to commit offenses under aggravated circumstances with terrorist aims, and of organized violence at the protests. His wife is also suspected of the same offenses but was not arrested.
Sihar was also known to Italy 's domestic intelligence service. The service flagged him as early as 2024, after he founded an organization called Rising Dawn. According to the report, the group spread propaganda identified with Hamas and with the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine in Muslim communities across Europe.
Sihar studied communications and political science at the University of Milan, and his thesis examined Islamist movements in Morocco. While a student, he headed the university's Muslim students' association. In 2024, he completed an internship at the international research institute ISPI, which hurried to clarify on Saturday that he has not worked with it since. He has also written in the past for the Il Fatto Quotidiano website about Tunisia, the Palestinians and the war in Iran.
According to ANSA , Sihar is a longtime pro-Palestinian activist. On October 7, 2023, he responded to a tweet by Deputy Prime Minister Matteo Salvini, who had expressed support for Israel, with the words "Allahu Akbar." On his profile, he wrote, "We will not stop fighting until we recover every inch of our land." In posts he published around pro-Palestinian demonstrations, he added, "We will not surrender, we will win or die."
On Saturday morning, before the protests, police also conducted more than 150 home searches in Milan and 20 other cities, most of them in the north of the country. The searches followed a WhatsApp group discovered on the phone of one of the suspects in the previous week's riots. "Bro, calm down, we are all against the police," read one of the messages. The group also contained messages about plans to attack police officers, steal their weapons and set buildings on fire.
According to La Repubblica , it remains unclear who is behind the movement. The calls for the first protests were spread online by an anonymous group called Italy in the Streets, which called for protests over the cost of living and "starvation wages." Anti-vaccine activists, students and even far-right groups came to the protests, but teenagers took center stage, many of them from poor neighborhoods and children of immigrants. After the riots, an Instagram page called the October 17 Movement appeared and tried to unify the protests in the various cities.
In Milan, where the government sent 500 soldiers, more than 10,000 people marched, according to La Repubblica , and about 2,000 marched in Florence. Most protests passed quietly, but clashes with police erupted in Rome, Turin, Bologna and Florence. Police said nine people were arrested across Italy and 371 were detained, 110 of them minors.
The heaviest clashes were recorded in Turin and Bologna. In Turin, masked youths hurled stones and bottles at police, who responded with volleys of tear gas and water cannons. Several young people were reportedly injured.
Alongside the protest over fuel prices, leftist slogans against the rise in the defense budget were also heard. In Turin, protesters chanted in French the slogan widespread at the demonstrations in France, "Everyone hates the police." In Rome, protesters tried to reach government buildings, and police pushed them back with water cannons. Another group entered the Colosseum.
According to La Repubblica , neo-fascist groups and extremist soccer fans have also expressed readiness to take to the streets and confront the protesters. The same report said a group of about 30 young people marched in Milan and shouted insults against Muslims.
Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni thanked the security forces, who "worked to ensure the safety of citizens and the right to protest peacefully, despite attempts by some violent individuals to provoke clashes and riots." She said the measures the government approved in recent days were meant to give the country more effective tools and "prevent criminals and troublemakers from setting whole cities on fire." Interior Minister Matteo Piantedosi warned, "the strength of the state sooner or later presents the bill."
In Barcelona, at least 100 people were also arrested, 27 of them minors. According to the Catalan news site La Vanguardia , the protest was organized on social media, inspired by the wave of protest in France.
The protest was reportedly called Angry High Schoolers, after the movement leading the student protests in France, and eyewitnesses told La Vanguardia that some of the rioters spoke French among themselves. The young people hurled fireworks at police and smashed bus stops, and when police charged them, they scattered through nearby streets. Dozens of them tried to break into stores, and hundreds of shoppers were trapped in stores that closed their doors.
The newspaper's reporter on the scene described the rioters as "teenagers, some under 14, and many girls as well," moving in groups of about 10. The reporter said, "Most of them seem confused, but there are a few older guys coordinating the looting." Salvador Illa, head of Catalonia's autonomous government, wrote on social media that violence has "no place in Catalonia" and thanked the police.
In France, hundreds of thousands of people continued to protest on Saturday against the cost of living, a week after riots in the country spiraled out of control. According to the Interior Ministry, 410,000 people took part in the protests, while the CGT labor union estimated the number at 800,000.
In Paris and a series of other cities, police fired tear gas at protesters, and according to Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez, nearly 1,000 people were arrested. Two people were seriously injured, one of them a young man in Toulouse who was hit in the hand. In Marseille and Grenoble, stores were looted, and in Cannes and Montpellier, far-right activists took to the streets to confront far-left activists.
Nuñez described the outcome as more "positive" than the previous week's, thanks to a larger police presence. Far-left leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who marched in Paris, said of President Emmanuel Macron, "He will understand that this will happen again every week." The Yellow Vests, a French grassroots protest movement, have already called for another protest on October 31.

articles.content_orig:
Bright Lake Wealth Management founder Ted Thatcher analyzes how election anxiety and uncertainty impacts the markets and what it means for investors on 'Varney & Co.'
Nelson Peltz's Trian Fund Management on Wednesday made an offer to buy Wendy's for roughly $1.4 billion in a move that would make the fast-food chain a privately held company.
Trian has been a long-term shareholder in Wendy's and Peltz's hedge fund is leading a group that offered to buy the struggling fast food giant at a price of $7.35 a share in cash.
The $1.4 billion bid to purchase Wendy's is about a 20% premium over the company's valuation of $1.2 billion at Tuesday's market close.
The offer by the Trian-led group was confirmed by FOX Business and disclosed in a filing on Wednesday. The Wall Street Journal first reported on the offer.
WENDY'S LOSES STATUS AS SECOND-LARGEST BURGER CHAIN AFTER 6-YEAR RUN
Wendy's stock has struggled over the last five years. (Mike Campbell/NurPhoto via Getty Images)
Wendy's shares have fallen about 68% over the last five years as of Wednesday's market open, though the stock surged nearly 17% on Wednesday morning following the news.
The Trian-led group bidding to buy Wendy's includes restaurant operator Flynn Group along with investment firms BlueFive Capital and Sixth Street Partners.
The group said in a letter that making Wendy's a private company would better allow it to carry out a complicated turnaround process that's expected to take multiple years and entail major capital investment .
MAJOR WENDY'S FRANCHISEE FILES FOR BANKRUPTCY
Nelson Peltz, founder and CEO of Trian Fund Management, said in the letter that Wendy's would be better positioned as a private company. (Marco Bello/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
"Wendy's sits at a critical juncture. The external environment has become increasingly challenging given the significant pressures on the U.S. consumer , economic uncertainty, persistent commodity inflation and intensifying competition, particularly with the QSR burger category," the group wrote.
"The business requires significant capital investment to de-lever and execute the strategic initiatives needed to turn system performance around," it added.
WENDY'S TO CLOSE HUNDREDS OF RESTAURANTS AS COMPANY LOOKS TO FOCUS ON VALUE TO BOOST SALES
The letter said that in the group's view, the alternative to accepting the offer to take Wendy's private is "continued exposure to market volatility while the Company works to manage its balance sheet against approaching debt maturities and the significant capital investment needed for the brand, all under the short-term pressure of public markets ."
"We believe private ownership is the better path and provides the patient, long-duration capital needed to restore the business and the franchise system to a position of strength," the group added.

articles.content_orig:
Fox News is suffering a catastrophic drop in viewership, which has plunged to historic lows just before the midterm elections, according to new data.
Preliminary Nielsen ratings obtained by Status ahead of their official release show that the Trump-friendly juggernaut is on track to post its lowest-rated month in total day viewers since December 2023, averaging just 1.1 million total viewers throughout October 2026. However, last yearâs ratings were buoyed by huge stories, including the Gaza ceasefire and the hostage release.
Among the key 25-54 demographic coveted by advertisers, the outlet is headed for its lowest-rated month in a quarter-century, averaging a paltry 98,000 viewers. It places third in that group, and fifth among 18-49 demos.
The collapse represents a brutal 27 percent drop in total viewers and a 32 percent dive in the 25-54 demographic compared to last October.
Even early-morning institution âFox & Friendsâ marked its second straight month below 1 million total viewers.
Fox is still the only network to average over one million in total day viewers for October. But while the network still leads overall cable ratings ahead of sports broadcast giant ESPN, even despite the return of football, the sudden drop-off might signal a stark reality for Republicans heading into next Tuesdayâs vote.
With Donald Trumpâs approval ratings stuck near historic lows, conservative interest appears to be cratering right when party bosses need enthusiasm the most.
By clicking â SUBSCRIBE â you agree to our Terms of Use and Privacy Policy .
The ratings slide extends straight into prime timeâthe crucial 8 p.m. to 11 p.m. block managed by network chief Suzanne Scott under executive chairman Rupert Murdoch.
Fox News is averaging 2 million total primetime viewers, representing a 28 percent drop from last year, while falling 36 percent in the key demographic down to 183,000 viewers. The figures confirm that even the networkâs marquee evening stars are failing to keep core Republican voters engaged.
Even early morning institution Fox & Friends âtraditionally a staple of Trumpâs personal daily viewing routineâmarked its second consecutive month below 1 million total viewers and under 100,000 in the key demographic.
October registered as the morning flagshipâs worst performance in overall viewers since July 2015, and its lowest in the 25-54 demographic since June 2001.
Meanwhile, competitor networks are capitalizing on the shift. Progressive rival MS NOW, which Trump despises, expanded its daytime audience by 16 percent to 588,000 total viewers compared to last year. CNN, which Trump also despises, registered a 3 percent bump up to 402,000 daytime viewers over the same timeframe.
The ratings collapse coincides with escalating tension between Trump and his long-preferred news outlet.
Trump publicly slammed Fox News on Truth Social for airing interviews with Democratic candidates like Michigan Senate contender Abdul El-Sayed, Kentucky Senate candidate Charles Booker, and Iowa gubernatorial nominee Rob Sand, complaining that Republican figures were getting âblurred outâ by the traditional media.
âFoxNews is spending far too much time putting on the OPPONENTS of Republican Party Candidates, people that love our Country, and have Great Policies and Ideas,â Trump posted, accusing the network of âtrying too hard to be Politically Correct.â
Trump also raged after Fox News briefly cut back on live coverage of his signature campaign rallies, encouraging supporters to switch to Right Side Broadcast News (RSBN), the far-right outlet launched by Trump enthusiast Joe Seales in 2015 to stream rallies uninterrupted.
Even the primetime slot, which includes network heavyweights like Sean Hannity, is failing to deliver.
Behind the scenes at network headquarters, insiders suggest the programming choices reflect audience fatigue. Speaking on condition of anonymity, a Fox host told CNN that directives come straight from executives, noting the internal consensus is simple: âTrump doesnât rate anymore.â
However, with polls poised to open in a matter of days, the network has begun to switch the president back on. It aired his Texas rally live on Tuesday.
Fox News has been asked to comment on the Nielsen data.

articles.title_orig: 8BitDo’s new Xbox Elite-style controller sets a high bar for customization
articles.title_zh: 8BitDo’s new Xbox Elite-style controller sets a high bar for customization
articles.content_orig:
The retro controller maker’s first real swing at a premium controller feels great, but it doesn’t earn its high price tag.
The retro controller maker’s first real swing at a premium controller feels great, but it doesn’t earn its high price tag.
If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.
It’s hard to make an Xbox controller that stands out these days, especially one that’s expensive, due to a wealth of great semi-affordable options. Still, 8BitDo’s $150 Ultimate 3E is a bold controller that holds its own against other feature-packed options. It’s made for Xbox and PC gamers who want a deeper level of customization and a more refined design than Microsoft’s pricier Xbox Elite Series 2 and 8BitDo’s own $60 Ultimate 2 .
Basically every feature I’m looking for in a controller is here, plus some, including drift-proof TMR joysticks, extra shoulder buttons, rear paddles, motion control support, modular buttons and joysticks, a 3.5mm audio jack for chat or private listening, and a 1,000Hz polling rate over a low-latency wireless connection (only when connected to a PC). It includes a carrying case and a wireless charging dock that you can stash the USB dongle within.
8BitDo’s first premium controller competes directly with other big names, like Razer, PowerA, SteelSeries , and rising star GameSir. But the Ultimate 3E is also among the most expensive of the bunch, and I’m not sure the company delivers enough additional features to pull it off.
The Ultimate 3E’s modular design opens up more customization than a lot of other controllers I’ve tried. It includes two four-button modules (one with membrane buttons and another with clickier microswitch buttons), two directional pads, and three extra joysticks. That level of customization and included accessories should hopefully help it age more gracefully than cheaper alternatives.
Its TMR joystick mechanisms shouldn’t wear down, so you’ll only need to be concerned with replacing the joystick tops down the line, and the controller includes several to choose from. However, 8BitDo doesn’t sell replacement accessories for the Ultimate 3E, as it does for many of its other controllers , and it hasn’t responded to The Verge as to whether it ever will.
The Ultimate 3E’s modularity also helps somewhat to make up for the high price tag. 8BitDo’s Pro 3 already lets you swap individual magnetically attaching buttons to accommodate different console layouts. The Ultimate 3E doesn’t offer as much freedom of per-button placement as the Pro 3, likely due to being intended for use with Xbox and PC, but the joy of using its microswitch button module makes up for the limitation. They’re sharp and clicky, although they have a bit more travel than I’d like.
My other complaints are relatively minor. The clips that hold the face button module in place are very tight, and I found myself having to carefully use a plastic toothpick to pop them out. Similarly, swapping out joysticks requires a surprising amount of force, and I had to work up the courage to yank them off the first time. And, even when set to their higher response point, the triggers feel a bit soft and, like the membrane buttons, have more travel than I prefer, although the extra shoulder button can offset that travel distance in some situations. The soft touch grips and back gather dust and gunk pretty quickly, but you can at least clean the joystick tops by removing them.
It’s as weird of a time to be releasing a new high-end Xbox controller as it is shopping for one. Assuming you’re not content with the solid but basic Microsoft model that’s around $50, it seems unwise to commit to spending well over $100 on one given the increased frequency of Xbox Elite Series 3 leaks . What we’ve seen of that, while unofficial, seems interesting: It doesn’t appear to offer the modular customization of the Ultimate 3E, but its screen and knobs might be what some people want in their next controller.
As for how the Ultimate 3E stacks up to other great controllers, Microsoft’s Elite Series 2 is a poor value by comparison. It uses potentiometer joysticks that are likely to drift over time, which to me feels disqualifying given the price point. I don’t think anyone using 8BitDo’s Ultimate 2 should feel the urge to upgrade to the Ultimate 3E. There just aren’t enough differences to make it worthwhile. However, there’s also a non-modular 8BitDo Ultimate 3 for $99, which may end up being a sweet spot for more budget-conscious gamers who don’t need to tinker as much.
For what it’s worth, I’ll be sitting down with the GameSir G7 Pro to play GTA VI . It’s one of my favorite Xbox controllers, and it has a nearly identical set of features and specs to the 8BitDo. Better yet, it’s only $80 at full price and comes in a variety of colors, with swappable faceplates for sale.
Overall, the Ultimate 3E feels similar to use as other Elite-style controllers I’ve tried, and that’s impressive for a company that hasn’t tried to take on pricier competition before. Whether you opt for the cheaper Ultimate 3 with mostly similar specs or the pricier, more customizable Ultimate 3E, 8BitDo’s high-end gamepads make a strong impression, but they’re tough to recommend when there are cheaper alternatives that don’t slack on features.

articles.title_orig: EU set to scrap ‘associate member’ offer for Canada
articles.title_zh: EU set to scrap ‘associate member’ offer for Canada
articles.content_orig:
BRUSSELS — EU countries have dropped the idea of offering Canada "associate member" status in the 27-member bloc, opting instead for softer language promising "ever closer association" ahead of a landmark EU-Canada summit, according to the latest version of the draft statement, seen by POLITICO.
A group of countries including Germany, Greece and France all objected to mentioning associate membership in a joint EU-Canada statement to be issued in Montreal, the diplomats said.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen had originally proposed "associate membership" for Canada in her State of the European Union speech in September, catching some EU countries off-guard.
A previous draft of the joint statement had read that the EU and Canada would "work to define by the 2027 EU-Canada Summit the concept of Associate Member that will reflect, through this even closer association, our common endeavour and cooperation towards our shared goals of prosperity, economic security and strategic autonomy."
In the final version, the text reads: "We will create an even closer association between Canada and the EU... and work to define by the 2027 EU-Canada Summit the concept of an ever closer association of Canada to the EU, short of full membership itself."
Later in the statement, the language changes from "even closer" to "ever closer." The text still needs final approval. EU countries have a deadline of 6 p.m. to raise objections.
While countries disagree over the wording to describe the relationship, Brussels is not softening its offering to Canada of a vastly expanded partnership.
“The good news is it doesn’t matter about specific names or nomenclature," Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said Tuesday. "What matters is the difference that it will make to lives of Canadians."

Mortgage broker Marcus Tzaferis says today's rate decision might not do much to weigh on the housing market by keeping new buyers on the sidelines, because so many Canadians are already choosing not to buy.
But it will weigh on mortgage holders.
Those with variable rates will feel it the most. On a $500,000 mortgage, a rate hike of 25 basis points would add about $70 per month on average to a holder's monthly payments.
While that might not seem like much, Tzaferis says Canadians are already struggling with the high cost of living, pointing to a rise in insolvencies as a sign consumers are having a tough time.
"To a consumer that's already stretched, these 25 basis point incremental increases are going to have an impact," Tzaferis said.
For variable rate holders who are thinking about the impact that rising rates could have and want more predictability, Tzaferis says "now is the time" to try and lock in a fixed mortgage.
And for those who will need to renegotiate a mortgage within the next year, Tzaferis says they have the option to lock in a fixed rate further in advance, "almost like an insurance policy for themselves," which could make sense for some.
Pedro Antunes, chief economist at independent research firm Signal 49, says he thinks the bank could have held off longer before raising rates.
Looking at last month's inflation numbers, Antunes says inflation from oil still hasn't started spilling over into the cost of other prices yet. While the overall 3.1 inflation rate was high, core measures that strip out volatile items like oil were much lower and within the bank's target range.
"We haven't seen … a broader-based increase in prices, but I think that the bank has started to be concerned about what's coming down the road," Antunes told CBC News.
And that concern is somewhat warranted, he said, especially after the bank didn't raise rates quickly in the face of high inflation post-COVID. The signal today is that the bank doesn't want a redo of that.
"I think the bank is concerned about this oil price shock playing a role here in the same way that it did in 2022. And you know, who can blame them? They're a little nervous about how that might play out."
Here’s why you’re paying more for diesel
Crude oil exports through the Strait of Hormuz are slowly recovering, so why is the price of diesel skyrocketing? The National's Eli Glasner breaks down what’s causing the increase, and why diesel prices likely won't drop anytime soon.
Rising oil prices linked to war in the Middle East have been a persistent irritant for the Bank of Canada as it attempts to control inflation. That war could escalate in the coming weeks.
U.S. officials have told several Gulf Arab countries to be prepared for a short, intense military campaign after the U.S. midterm elections on Nov. 3, the Wall Street Journal reported on Wednesday .
The U.S. benchmark oil price soared nearly 3.5 per cent today, rising above $103 US per barrel. West Texas Intermediate crude is up nearly 70 per cent year-over-year.
According to data from Kalibrate, Canadian pump prices for regular gasoline are up nearly 30 per cent on average versus this time last year. Diesel prices have soared over 70 per cent on an annualized basis.
Here's what the Bank of Canada said about the situation earlier today:
"The conflict in the Middle East is now in its eighth month, and there is no clear path to resolution. The combination of higher-for-longer energy prices, and increased pass-through, adds to the persistence of inflation in the projection.
"The prices of gasoline, diesel and heating oil are considerably higher than in July, and are expected to remain higher for longer. This is hitting consumers directly and raising business costs for production and transportation."
Benjamin Reitzes, managing director at BMO Economics, says the central bank's messaging indicates further hikes will come — but maybe not soon.
Despite the Bank of Canada warning that more rate hikes might be necessary, it also said it would proceed with caution. That "suggests a follow-up hike in December isn't a lock by any means," Reitzes said.
"There's likely more tightening to come, but the pace of further hikes is extremely uncertain and will be driven by the incoming data," he wrote in a note to investors.
Reitzes says weak growth forecasted for the last few months of this year and continued trade uncertainty will be the things to watch — and that if momentum picks up there, that could trigger more increases.
Heading into today's decision, business owners across Canada were already in a tough spot.
The trade war with the U.S. has been a significant weight and increased the cost of doing business, according to Simon Gaudreault, chief economist for the Canadian Federation of Independent Business (CFIB).
"We're talking about entrepreneurs that have been entrepreneurs for 15, 20, 25 years or more, telling us that they've never seen such a challenging situation in terms of the operating costs," Gaudreault said.
Today's rate hike could add to that pain for lots of businesses, he said. A rate hike would leave Canadian consumers with less cash in their pockets, which Gauldreaut says could hurt demand for business owners.
Many business owners also have variable mortgages for business properties or hold other kinds of debt at floating rates, he said, meaning their costs will now be higher. It could also make it harder to take on new business investments, like upgrading equipment.
"The trade war hasn't brought that sort of certainty that you're looking for as an entrepreneur to invest. And so making the cost of capital even higher, even more expensive with the rate hike certainly won't help here."

Bank of Canada senior deputy governor Carolyn Rogers, speaking after the central bank hiked a key interest rate, said the organization's outlook for housing is 'pretty subdued' for a few reasons, including overall economic uncertainty.
Deputy governor Carolyn Rogers acknowledged that the bank's interest rate hike will add to pressures on homebuyers.
"Certainly borrowing rates are currently weighing a bit on the housing market. An increase will add to that a bit on the margin," Rogers said.
She said the bank expects Canada's housing market to remain sluggish over the next two years.
Rogers said the bank's outlook for housing remains "pretty subdued," with growth forecast at about one per cent over the next two years.
"There's a number of things weighing on housing right now," Rogers said, pointing to broader uncertainty in the economy caused by inflation, energy costs and trade issues.
"People don't tend to make big purchase decisions like housing in that kind of an environment."
Rogers said the housing market is undergoing an adjustment, with particularly sharp slowdowns in British Columbia and Ontario, especially in Vancouver and Toronto.

Korean memory chipmaker SK Hynix (NASDAQ:SKHY) reported its fiscal 2026 third-quarter results, and investors were clearly impressed. The company reported record revenue of 104.6 trillion South Korean Won (roughly $78.9 billion), up 328% year over year and 32% quarter over quarter. At the same time, operating profit of 83.3 trillion won (roughly $61.7 billion) soared 632% year over year and 38% sequentially.
For context, analysts' consensus estimates called for revenue of 98.34 trillion won and operating profit of about 76.7 trillion won, so the results easily surpassed investor expectations.
However, what really turned heads was management commentary about the state of the industry. SK Hynix's outlook speaks volumes: "Demand [is] expected to outpace supply through 2030." The company also noted that its supply is essentially sold out for the next three years. There have been fears that demand for memory chips would begin to decline starting in 2028, so this pronouncement was cheered by investors.
The company also announced that it would return 100 trillion won to shareholders, including at least 30 trillion won in cash dividends and 60 trillion won via share buybacks.
As one of the Big Three computer memory manufacturers, Micron will benefit from the ongoing demand for High-Bandwidth Memory (HBM), Dynamic Random-Access Memory (DRAM), and NAND flash memory chips -- all critical to the ongoing adoption of artificial intelligence (AI).
Despite stock price gains of more than 340% over the past year (as of this writing), Micron stock is selling for just 13 times earnings, a valuation that is all the more attractive given that the company continues to deliver revenue and profit growth in the triple digits. Moreover, SK Hynix seemed to confirm that the current demand cycle will continue for several more years, and Micron has adopted measures to lock its major customers into multi-year, non-cancelable contracts, thus ensuring the boon continues.
That's why Micron stock is still a buy.

Continuing its fast-paced experiments with AI apps, Meta has now launched a new app called Waddle World, which essentially looks like a Tamagotchi clone, but with AI. The might be a test, but it could very well be a precursor to the company’s Tamagotchi-like gadget powered by Muse .
The company has launched Waddle World in the Philippines on both iOS and Android. The app, spotted by social media consultant Matt Navarra , lets you pick and grow a virtual pet, feed it, and play with it.
We have reached out to Meta for a comment on wider availability, and will update this piece if we hear back.

Meta’s description of the app indicates that it doesn’t want the app to be a habit builder. The company’s page also says that the app is not a chatbot, and is flagged as suitable for users older than 18.
“Waddle World is a cozy 16-bit world where your pixel pet lives. Hatch a virtual pet, visit whenever you like, and let it get to know you. No pressure, no streaks to protect, no scores to chase — just a warm little escape in the cracks of your day,” the app’s description reads.
“Not a chatbot. Not an assistant. Not a productivity tool. It’s a pet, and a place. Stay two minutes or twenty — it’ll be happy either way.”
The app also doubles as a journal, letting users describe their day through voice or text. The pet listens to the user and writes up the note in its own voice as an entry with a doodle. The app also features mini-games that you can play over a few minutes, and can send you a weekly email based on what it learned about you.
Meta may be wanting to stay away from building companion apps, given companies like Character.AI and OpenAI have faced lawsuits that allege their products caused harm to teenagers.
Until now, the social media giant has released AI-centric apps like Pocket, which lets you vibe-code games , and Vibes, which let you quickly generate videos .

Shares of Stellantis were up Wednesday as the European car giant's third-quarter results showed it was making progress with its 60 billion euro turnaround plan.
Third-quarter revenues rose 1% to 37.6 billion euros from a year ago, the Chrysler and Jeep owner said on Wednesday, while adjusted operating income rose 184% to 256 million euros from 90 million euros a year earlier.
The automaker's industrial free cash flow improved to negative 4 billion euros, up from negative 4.3 billion the year prior.
Stellantis on Wednesday also reconfirmed its 2026 guidance and target to achieve positive free cash flow next year, which is a main focus for investors.
"Q3 was soft, but consensus expectations were far lower. Key here is that '26 Guidance was maintained while other auto OEMs and suppliers are cutting on elevated costs," RBC Capital Markets analyst Tom Narayan said Wednesday in an investor note.
Stellantis stock rose roughly 9% Wednesday in Milan and was up by 12% in early trading in New York, but it remains sharply down since the beginning of the year.
Stellantis CEO Antonio Filosa told investors Wednesday that the company is ahead of schedule on its turnaround plan, which was announced in May. He said Stellantis expects to exceed its previously announced cost-cutting efforts of 6 billion euros under the plan by 2028, including 2.4 billion euros to start 2027.
"We are very confident in reaffirming our '26 guidance. Those include '27 free cash flow positive," Filosa said Wednesday in response to concerns about the carmaker's ability to achieve its free cash flow target.
Stellantis' 2026 guidance includes a mid-single-digit percentage increase in net revenue and a low-single-digit adjusted operating margin.
Stellantis' turnaround plan includes investing 36 billion euros in its portfolio of automotive brands, with 60% of the cash to go towards its struggling North America sector. It also plans to introduce new vehicles, refresh models, and incorporate new technologies in its products.
Stellantis is targeting roughly 23% revenue growth, from 154 billion euros last year to 190 billion euros by 2030, with a 7% adjusted operating margin by then.
European carmakers, including Stellantis, have been struggling in China as domestic brands like Xiaomi, BYD and Geely gain ground and intensify competition.
Just this week, German luxury carmaker Porsche said it would reduce its exposure to China as car sales decline in the region. Meanwhile, Mercedes-Benz said its third-quarter car sales slumped due to a "challenging market environment," in the country.
Earlier this month, Filosa told CNBC that European regulators need to do more to incentivize carmakers to manufacture vehicles in the region to fend off Chinese rivals.
Filosa called for regulation that "incentivizes, rewards, and protects the ones that are able to demonstrate that they design cars, engineer cars."

articles.title_orig: Dutch zookeeper dies after being attacked by leopard
articles.title_zh: Dutch zookeeper dies after being attacked by leopard
articles.content_orig:
A zookeeper has died from her injuries days after she was attacked by a leopard at the Dutch safari park where she worked.
The unnamed employee, who had worked at the Beekse Bergen safari park for almost four decades, was attacked by the animal on Saturday and died on Tuesday.
“With enormous sadness, we have to report that the animal caretaker of safari park Beekse Bergen passed away today from the injuries she sustained on Saturday, October 24, in an incident with a leopard in the park,” the park said in a statement Tuesday.
“Her passing also deeply affects us all, and we are intensely grieving with her family, friends and loved ones. We ask for peace and privacy for her loved ones and our staff, so that they can process this profound loss,” the statement added.
The woman suffered serious wounds to her head and neck while working in an enclosure with two male Persian leopards, the Associated Press reported.
The woman contacted colleagues via a walkie talkie after the incident in the leopard’s enclosure and an ambulance and trauma helicopter were dispatched at around 11 a.m. local time Saturday, AP added. She underwent emergency surgery but her condition worsened on Sunday evening.
The employee joined the park, located in the southern Netherlands, when she was 17 years old and had worked there “with short breaks for almost 40 years,” the park’s statement added.
CNN affiliate NOS reported that the zookeeper had been working with the leopards for eight years and had been working alone in the enclosure with two male Persian leopards when she was attacked.
There are no cameras inside the enclosure, the park told NOS, which also reported that the animals have been treated as normal since the incident.
The park said that an independent investigation had been launched into the woman’s death.
Rhino kills zookeeper and seriously injures another in Austria
Home to more than 100 species of animals, Beekse Bergen offers visitors the choice of seeing the safari park by foot, car, bus and boat.
This is not the first time a member of staff at a zoo or safari park has been fatally injured by an animal.
In 2023, a zookeeper was killed in Austria after being attacked by a rhino. The incident, in which another zookeeper was injured, occurred at Salzburg Hellbrunn Zoo. Two years prior to that, a woman working at a safari park in Chile was killed by a tiger while working in the big cats’ enclosure.
CNN’s Rose Roobeek contributed to this report.

Frontier Airlines reported a 71% increase in airfare in the third quarter as the country's largest budget airline tried to pass along an even bigger jump in jet fuel prices.
Frontier's fare revenue averaged $67.82 per passenger in the third quarter, compared with $39.74 last year. Including the budget airline's many fees, such as for checked and carry-on luggage, total revenue per passenger rose 30% on the year to $138.22.
Customers kept booking despite the higher prices. Frontier's passenger count rose 18% to more than 9.8 million people in the quarter. That's a difference of 1.5 million passengers from last year.
The company said demand remains strong, even at these higher prices, but Frontier still lost money. The airline widened its third-quarter loss to $104 million from a $77 million loss a year earlier. Its fuel bill soared 82% to $425 million.
Frontier forecast potential adjusted profit in the fourth quarter, saying it expects to post an adjusted loss of 15 cents per share to adjusted earnings of as much as 5 cents per share.
Carriers from Delta Air Lines to Frontier have said customers are mostly continuing to book flights despite higher fares, but that record jet fuel prices, their biggest cost after labor, are eroding profits.
Frontier shares were up more than 9% in afternoon trading Wednesday.
Frontier had eclipsed Spirit Airlines as the biggest discount carrier in the country even before that airline collapsed in May.

An ​attacker with two knives who wounded a policeman guarding the Israeli embassy in Belgrade overnight has been shot dead.
Serbia's outgoing interior minister confirmed the news on Wednesday.
“One minor, of so far undetermined identity, who is reasonably suspected to be from Šabac, ⁠rushed at an ​officer of the ⁠Gendarmerie shouting ‘Allahu Akbar’ and attacked him with two knives,” Ivica Dacic ⁠said in an emailed statement.
Dacic added that ​he ⁠had raised Serbia's ‌security threat level to red, the highest, and that there would be an increased police ‌presence at key locations. ‌The officer suffered a light head wound, Dacic said.
It is the second such attack at Belgrade's ⁠Israeli embassy in two years. In June 2024, an assailant shot a Serbian police officer with a crossbow.
The attack came a day after Israelis went to the polls, with projected results showing the ‌opposition bloc neck and neck ​with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's camp.
Israel's Central Elections Committee was tallying votes on Wednesday and it will likely take until Thursday before definitive results of the election - the first since the Hamas-led attack of October 7, 2023 - are known.
With some 48.4% of votes tallied, Netanyahu's bloc was projected to ⁠win 55 seats, and Eisenkot's bloc 50 seats, with 15 seats going to Arab parties, Israeli media reported, a distribution will likely change as more votes are tallied.
That leaves both sides short of the 61 seats needed for a majority in the 120-seat Knesset, and neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot claimed victory.
Serbia's ‌student-led movement toppled longtime ⁠leader Aleksandar Vucic in an election ⁠on Sunday, but the outgoing administration remains in place ‌in a ​caretaker role until the new ‌government is formed.
Protesters entered a Serbian television station supportive of Vucic late on Monday, interrupting broadcasting to call for the arrest of its editor, as tens of thousands took to the streets for ⁠a second night of post-election celebrations.
Serbia's Student List, born out of a student-led anti-corruption protest movement, unseated Vucic in a historic election, bringing to an end 14 years in power for a man who served as information minister under Slobodan Milosevic and who maintained tight control over the media.
Live footage broadcast by Informer TV showed around 30 people walk ⁠into its newsroom on Monday evening and surround editor-in-chief and owner ​Dragan ⁠Vucicevic. Some protesters shouted: "This is how it is in free Serbia" and "Where is Vucic now?" Some also called for Vucicevic's arrest.
On his personal Instagram account, Vucic, dressed in a jumper displaying the ⁠crossed-out word "sorry", called the event an attack on free speech and the freedom of journalism.
